description: A little bit of science, a little bit of art, and probably way too many ideas at once! We’re a team passionate about the intersection of science, creativity, and video games. We’re always happy to welcome new minds to the team! We’re especially looking for people with skills or interests in digital art, illustration, graphic design, UI/UX, AI, and game development. If you enjoy making things, experimenting, and adding your own creative touch to a team, we’d love to have you along!
summary: Marswalk is an interactive planning tool that helps astronauts decide when, where and how to take a walking excursion on Mars. Set in Gale Crater, where NASA’s Curiosity rover operates, it combines open data: rover air temperatures from REMS, USGS terrain models, HiRISE imagery via NASA Mars Trek, and Curiosity’s radiation and waypoint records. A Gaussian process forecasts temperature, validated against withheld data with 3.2 K average error, and a worst-case rule issues GO, CAUTION or NO-GO verdicts. An A* algorithm finds routes that avoid steep slopes, and the TRACE mission challenges users to reach hydrated minerals and return safely. Built with HTML, JavaScript and Leaflet, it runs offline in a web browser. Claude assisted our team as a development tool; we defined the concept, requirements and decisions. Communication delays of up to 24 minutes make on-site decisions essential, and Marswalk supports them with transparent, data-driven guidance.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Astertrail helps plan an astronaut’s walk on Mars before it happens. The user draws a route over real satellite imagery of Gale Crater from NASA Mars Trek and picks a departure time. The tool works out the air temperature on each segment at the moment the astronaut will reach it, along with its uncertainty. The route is colored by that temperature. A route profile chart shows elevation, slope, temperature and battery along the way. Using the terrain’s slope and the route’s curves, a simulator estimates the vehicle’s speed and energy use, including the heating power the cold demands. It ends with a verdict: GO, GO WITH CAUTION or NO-GO.

The temperature comes from real measurements by the REMS instrument on the Curiosity rover. That data has gaps and irregular sampling, so we trained and compared models to fill them. We tested our own neural network (VARnet-Marte) against a Gaussian Process (GP), checking each one against real readings we deliberately hid from it. The GP’s error was 3.2–3.9 K, so we chose it for accuracy. VARnet is about 475× faster, and we calibrated its uncertainty for large batches of queries in the future.

Benefits and expected impact

  • It decides based on the worst case, not the average. Each segment’s status uses the cold limit of the 95% interval, which is what matters for suit and battery safety.
  • It brings three risks that are usually analyzed separately into one view: cold, terrain and energy.
  • It shows how reliable each value is. When data is sparse, confidence drops and the tool says so.
  • For future crewed missions, it could reduce risk and help choose the safest route and time. As an educational tool, it brings real NASA data to students.

Tools and technologies

  • Python: PyTorch (VARnet-Marte neural network), scikit-learn (Gaussian Process), NumPy, pandas and SciPy. We used uv for the environment and trained on an NVIDIA RTX 4050 GPU (CUDA).
  • Real data: MSL REMS from the NASA PDS, WMTS imagery from NASA Mars Trek, and the USGS Astrogeology elevation model of Gale.
  • Interface: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no server, Leaflet for the map and custom canvas charts. It works offline.

What makes it creative?
The interface is designed as a spacecraft cockpit in pixel-art style. It has mission messages, a camera view that follows the astronaut, and playback at x1, x10 or x60 speed. This turns a scientific analysis into something easy to understand. The core idea is also original: temperature isn’t painted over the whole map but along the path, at the exact time of passage. That combines space and time in a single reading.

Factors our team considered

  • Honesty with data. REMS measures at a single point, so we didn’t invent a heat map of the whole area. Every number shows its source, and anything estimated is labeled as estimated.
  • Rigorous validation. We compared against baseline methods (linear, spline and GP) using error and uncertainty-coverage metrics, and we didn’t tune the baselines to lose.
  • Feasibility. We use precomputed data and an offline backup so the demo doesn’t depend on the internet.
  • Known limits. The model covers air temperature on open terrain. It doesn’t include shadows or ground temperature. Next steps are the geotopological map, already shown as “coming soon”, and an improved VARnet architecture.
